offence_severity: Minimum 10 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment or Death
physical_harm: Death of victim due to septicemia caused by gunshot injuries
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration recorded by the Executive Magistrate gave full details as to the identity of the assailants, the weapons used, the site of the injury and the fact that he was brought to the hospital by a neighbour and his elder brother who were accompanying him at the time of incident. The doctor who was looking after the deceased when the dying declaration was recorded gave a certificate that he was fully conscious and lucid at the time of its recording.
witness_credibility: The promptness in recording of FIR would belie the doubt as to the presence of eyewitness-informant at the place of incident. The presence of the two eye witnesses is accepted as they were accompanying the deceased to court and the promptness of the FIR reflects their presence.
trial_duration: The incident took place on 20th May 2000. The FIR was lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. The trial court judgment was on 8th August 2007. The High Court decision was on 8th August 2007. The Supreme Court judgment was on 5th May 2010.
legal_representation: Sushil Kumar, Manoj Prasad, Aditya Kumar for the Appellants. T.N. Singh, Rajiv Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra for the Respondent.
investigation_status: FIR lodged on 20th May 2000 at 12 noon. Charge-sheet filed. Trial completed.
appeal_history: Trial court acquitted the appellants of offence under Section 302 IPC but convicted them under Section 307 IPC. High Court convicted appellants for offence under Section 302/149 IPC. Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased, along with PW-1 and PW-2, was on the way to court to attend a case. The appellants armed with a pistol fired a shot at the deceased and then ran away. The deceased was seriously injured and taken to the hospital. The FIR was lodged promptly, and the presence of eyewitnesses was confirmed. The injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the first dying declaration recorded by the police officer did not have the endorsement of a doctor and was therefore unreliable. They also claimed that the second dying declaration was not properly endorsed and that the medical evidence showed the death was due to septicemia caused by the injuries, not the initial gunshot wound. They further argued that the eye witnesses were not present at the scene and that the case should be under Section 307 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate duly endorsed by a Doctor should not be discarded unless there are suspicious circumstances. The Court emphasized that the reliability of the dying declaration depends on the facts of the case and the evidence produced.
precedent_relied_upon: Balak Ram v. State of U.P. 1975(3) SCC 219; K. Ramachandra Reddy & Anr. v. The Public Prosecutor 1976(3) SCC 618
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death, and the dying declaration was reliable. The Court found that the trial court had erred in concluding that the doctor's negligence caused the death, and the High Court's conviction under Section 302/149 IPC was upheld.
